newsitem.title: INDIA: Gold-Indian sub-continent prices seen recovering.
newsitem.headline: Gold-Indian sub-continent prices seen recovering.

text.p: Gold prices in the Indian sub-continent are likely to improve this week, recovering from the subdued trend of the past fortnight, dealers said on Monday.

They said stabilising world prices and rising Indian demand could put some life into bullion trade in the sub-continent. The Bombay market was closed on Monday for Holi, the Hindu spring festival of colours.
In the week to Saturday, standard gold fell 60 rupees to 4,730 per 10 grammes and gold biscuits (116.50 grammes each) lost 700 rupees to 55,300.
Dealers said demand for gold had been subdued the last fortnight as it was considered inauspicious to buy precious metals in that period.
They said the week to Saturday had seen more supply than demand because of higher arrivals of imported gold and local sales of confiscated metal by the Customs department.
Dealers estimated supply during the week at around 400-500 kgs per day against the average of 300 kgs.

Bhayabhai Sanghavi, a leading bullion dealer, said a recent dip in world gold prices encouraged expatriate Indians to buy and bring in gold in larger quantities. Expatriate Indians are allowed to bring in up to 10 kgs of gold subject to an import duty of 220 rupees per 10 grammes.
Sanghavi said the premium for acquiring a special import licence (SIL) to import gold had come down to 10 percent at the beginning of the week from 13.5 percent the week before.
The SIL premium has since risen to 12 percent.
Traders who earn foreign exchange through exports are entitled to an SIL, which is tradable and commands a premium if supply is low and demand high. Most local bullion dealers acquire these licences.
"World gold prices have since stabilised at better levels. This should make imports costlier," Sanghavi said, adding that he would also expect a drop in the sale of gold by customs.
"I expect the market to improve," Sanghavi said.
The Indian spring festival also heralds the harvesting of summer crops, which improves villagers' incomes.
"The rural population opts for gold to put part of their savings in," said bullion analyst Dinesh Parikh. "Gold has touched the bottom. It can only rise."

Dealers in Pakistan's commercial city of Karachi said gold prices were expected to remain mixed this week because of low demand from jewellers. Low physical offtake of gold jewellery in the current wedding season would keep prices range-bound, one dealer said.
In the week to Saturday, prices of standard gold rose marginally by 21 rupees per 10 grammes to 4,749 rupees.
In Dubai, gold lost its shine after a strong run earlier this year, but traders expect business to pick up by April with the start of a month-long gold promotion fair.
"Pakistan is also slow," said a trader in the re-export business to the Indian subcontinent.
"Every year from about April to June trade to India and Pakistan slows down," said another.
